title: No-Code Builder Lab: Apps & Automation
blurb: Two career-changing skills in one lab: turn a web project into a real Android APK using only your browser (from the Team21 MaDSkillz manual), and build your first business automation with Make or Zapier — no code, no command line, ever.

modules.d: The concepts behind the clicks — repositories, automated builds, web-to-Android packaging and safe distribution.
modules.body:
Why understand what happens behind the buttons

This lab will take you from a downloaded project to an Android app installed on a phone, and to a working business automation — without writing code or using a command line. Builders who understand what each step does fix problems faster, explain their work confidently, and grow into more advanced roles. This module gives you the mental model.

GitHub: your project's home in the cloud

GitHub is a platform used by millions of developers to store, version and collaborate on software projects. Key ideas: a repository (repo) is a project folder with its full history; a commit is a saved snapshot of changes with a message describing them; every commit can be viewed or reverted later, which is your safety net. A public repository can be seen by anyone — required in this lab for free automated builds and public download links — so never place passwords, private keys or personal data in it.

Automated builds: CI/CD

Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) means that every time you change your project, machines automatically build (and can test and package) it. GitHub's CI/CD service is GitHub Actions. The instructions live in a workflow file inside the hidden .github folder of your project. When you upload that folder, GitHub reads the instructions and builds your Android app on its own servers — downloading Node.js, the Java development kit and the Android SDK, building the web app, syncing it into an Android project and producing the installable file. That is why the .github folder is critical: without it, nothing builds.

From web app to Android app. Your project is a web application (HTML, JavaScript and a framework such as React). A tool called Capacitor wraps that web app inside a native Android shell, so it runs like an installed app with an icon on the phone. The same approach can later produce iOS apps. Many real-world apps use this "web inside native" model.

APK, AAB and distribution

An APK (Android Package) is the file Android installs directly — perfect for testing and sharing within your community. The Google Play Store requires new apps to be submitted as an Android App Bundle (AAB), along with a developer account, signing keys and store listing requirements; that is a later step. Installing an APK from outside the Play Store is called sideloading: Android asks permission ("Install from this source") because apps from unknown sources can be unsafe. Only install APKs you trust — such as one you built yourself. Note that Google has announced developer verification requirements for apps installed on certified Android devices, phasing in from 2026 in some countries; if you plan wider distribution outside the Play Store, check the current rules.

No-code automation

The second half of this lab uses Make or Zapier to connect apps. Every automation has three parts: a trigger (the event that starts it — a new form response), one or more actions (what happens — send an email), and data mapping (passing information from the trigger into the action — the respondent's name and email). This trigger–action–mapping pattern underlies thousands of business automations.

What you will have by the end

  • A GitHub account hosting your project with full version history.
  • An automated system that builds a fresh Android APK every time you change your app.
  • An installed app on your phone and a public download link others can use.
  • A working business automation and the design skills to build more.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my no-code mentor. Explain in simple language, with an everyday analogy for each, what a repository, a commit, a workflow file, GitHub Actions, Capacitor, an APK and an AAB are. Then quiz me with 5 short questions to check I understand how a change in my project becomes a new installable app.

📚 Glossary

  • Repository: project folder with full version history
  • Commit: saved snapshot of changes with a message
  • CI/CD: automatic building, testing and delivery on every change
  • GitHub Actions: GitHub's automation service that runs workflows
  • Capacitor: tool wrapping a web app inside a native mobile shell
  • APK / AAB: Android installable package / Play Store submission format
  • Sideloading: installing apps from outside the Play Store

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual: From Zero to Android APK in One Hour. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Repositories, commits and GitHub Actions.
  • Capacitor documentation (capacitorjs.com).
  • Android Developers — Android App Bundles; developer verification announcements (verify current status).

quiz.q: A student uploads every project file except the hidden .github folder. What happens?
opts: No automated build runs, because the workflow instructions live in the .github folder
GitHub builds an iOS app instead
quiz.x: The workflow file in .github tells GitHub Actions how to build the APK.

quiz.q: Why must the repository be public in this lab?
opts: It enables the free automated builds and public download links used in the lab
GitHub requires all repositories to be public
quiz.x: The lab relies on free builds and public releases; public repos must therefore contain no secrets.

quiz.q: A learner wants to add a database password to a configuration file in the public repo. What is the BEST advice?
opts: Add it — only developers read repos
Add it in a commit message
Never place passwords or private data in a public repository
quiz.x: Anyone can read public repositories, including their history.

quiz.q: What does Capacitor do in this project?
opts: Wraps the web app inside a native Android shell so it installs and runs as an app
quiz.x: Capacitor packages web apps as native mobile apps.

quiz.q: A learner wants to publish the app on the Google Play Store. Which file format is required for new apps?
quiz.x: Google Play requires AAB for new app submissions.

quiz.q: Why does Android warn before installing an APK from outside the Play Store?
opts: Apps from unknown sources can be unsafe, so Android asks for permission
quiz.x: Sideloading warnings protect users from untrusted apps.

quiz.q: In a Make or Zapier automation, 'a new Google Form response' is the:
quiz.x: The trigger is the event that starts the automation.

quiz.q: Inserting the respondent's email address from the form into the 'To' field of an email is called:
quiz.x: Mapping passes data from the trigger into the action.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of commits for a beginner builder?
opts: They publish to the Play Store
They create a history of snapshots so mistakes can be reviewed and reverted
quiz.x: Version history is a safety net.

quiz.q: What does CI/CD mean in this lab?
opts: Manually building the app on your laptop
Machines automatically building and packaging the app whenever the project changes
quiz.x: GitHub Actions automates builds on every change.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK I: GitHub & Your Project
modules.d: Create your account, prepare your files with hidden folders visible, and create the repository correctly.
modules.body:
What you are about to do

Take a downloaded project file and turn it into a real Android app you can install on any phone — without touching a command line. First time through: about 45 minutes. Every time after: about 10 minutes.

Step 1 — Set up GitHub (5 min)

Open github.com in any modern browser and click Sign up. Use a real email address you check, a strong unique password, and a professional username — it becomes part of your public URLs (github.com/yourname) and potentially your professional portfolio. Verify the email code (check spam for messages from GitHub) and skip optional personalisation questions. Turn on two-factor authentication in your security settings — strongly recommended, and increasingly required by GitHub for contributors.

Step 2 — Prepare your files (3 min)

The project arrives as a compressed zip. Extract it: on Windows, right-click the zip in Downloads → Extract All → Extract; on Mac, double-click the zip. Open the extracted folder.

Critical: show hidden files. The project contains a .github folder. Names starting with a dot are hidden by default. Windows: in File Explorer, View → Show → Hidden items. Mac: press Command + Shift + . (period). The .github folder will appear slightly faded.

Critical checkpoint. Confirm you can SEE the .github folder before continuing. If you cannot see it, you cannot upload it — and your APK will never build. This single step causes more first-time failures than any other.

Understand what is in the folder

  • src — the app's source code, including App.jsx, which holds the app's text and interface.
  • public — static files such as icons and images.
  • package.json — the list of tools and libraries the project uses (do not edit unless you know why).
  • .github/workflows — the build instructions for GitHub Actions.
  • Capacitor configuration — settings for packaging the web app as an Android app (app name, ID).

Step 3 — Create the repository (5 min)

Signed in to GitHub, click the + icon (top right) → New repository. Name it in lowercase with dashes (for example madskillz-ai-readiness) — no spaces. Add a short description. Choose Public (required for free builds and public download links in this lab). Leave "Add a README", ".gitignore" and "license" unchecked — your project already contains its files, and adding them here creates conflicts. Click Create repository.

Naming and professionalism

Your repository and username are visible to anyone, including future employers and clients. Clear names, a description and later a README explaining what the app does make your work look professional and trustworthy.

Common mistakes at this stage

  • Uploading the zip file itself instead of the extracted contents.
  • Uploading the outer folder, so all files end up one level too deep.
  • Not showing hidden files, so .github is missed.
  • Ticking README or license options and creating conflicts.
  • Choosing Private, which blocks the lab's free public release links.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my GitHub setup guide. Walk me through creating my account, enabling two-factor authentication, showing hidden files on my operating system (I will tell you which), and creating my repository — one step at a time, waiting for me to confirm each step. At the end, give me a checklist to confirm the .github folder is visible and the repository settings are correct.

📚 Glossary

  • Two-factor authentication: second verification step protecting your account
  • Hidden files: files or folders starting with a dot, not shown by default
  • App.jsx: main app file holding text and interface
  • package.json: list of project tools and libraries
  • README: document explaining a project

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 1–3. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Creating a new repository; Configuring two-factor authentication.

quiz.q: A learner on Windows cannot see the .github folder. What should they do?
opts: In File Explorer, choose View → Show → Hidden items
quiz.x: Hidden items must be shown so the folder can be uploaded.

quiz.q: On a Mac, which keys show hidden files in a Finder window?
quiz.x: Command + Shift + period toggles hidden files.

quiz.q: When creating the repository, why should README, .gitignore and license be left unchecked?
opts: The project already contains its files, and adding them creates conflicts
quiz.x: Pre-created files conflict with the uploaded project.

quiz.q: Which repository name follows the lab's guidance?
quiz.x: Lowercase with dashes, no spaces.

quiz.q: A learner uploads the original .zip file to GitHub. What is the problem?
opts: Zip files make the repo private
The build needs the extracted files, not the compressed archive
quiz.x: The workflow expects the project's files and folders, not an archive.

quiz.q: Which file holds most of the app's visible text and interface?
quiz.x: App.jsx contains the app's text and interface.

quiz.q: Why does the course recommend enabling two-factor authentication?
opts: It protects your account and projects from unauthorised access
It is needed to install APKs
quiz.x: 2FA adds a second layer of account security.

quiz.q: Why should a learner choose a professional GitHub username?
opts: It cannot be seen by others
It appears in public URLs and may be seen by employers and clients
quiz.x: Your username is part of your public portfolio.

quiz.q: Files end up inside an extra folder level after upload (e.g., project/project/src). What likely happened?
opts: The outer folder was uploaded instead of its contents
quiz.x: Select and upload the contents, not the containing folder.

quiz.q: Which visibility setting does this lab require?
quiz.x: Public enables free builds and public releases used in the lab.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK II: Upload, Build & Install
modules.d: Upload correctly, watch GitHub Actions build your app, and install it on a phone.
modules.body:
Step 4 — Upload your project (10 min)

On your empty repository page, click the link "uploading an existing file". Arrange your project folder window and your browser side by side. Inside the project folder, select everything (Ctrl + A on Windows, Command + A on Mac) and confirm the .github folder is highlighted. Drag the selection into GitHub's upload area. If GitHub warns that a file is hidden, continue — it is supposed to be.

Scroll down to Commit changes, type a short message such as "Initial upload of project", and click Commit changes. Then verify on the repository page that src, public, .github and package.json appear at the top level.

Step 5 — Watch the build (Actions tab)

The moment .github lands, GitHub starts building your app. Click the Actions tab, then the run named "Build Android APK" (it may show a spinning yellow icon). Watch each step turn green:

  1. Checkout — GitHub copies your code to a build machine.
  2. Set up Node.js — the JavaScript runtime used to build the web app.
  3. Set up Java JDK — needed for Android builds.
  4. Set up Android SDK — Android's development toolkit.
  5. Install dependencies — the libraries listed in package.json.
  6. Build web app — compiles the app into optimised files (the dist folder).
  7. Capacitor sync — copies the web build into the Android project.
  8. Build APK — produces the Android package.
  9. Upload artifact — stores the APK for you to download.

The first build usually takes 5–10 minutes because GitHub downloads the full Android toolkit; later builds are faster. You can close the page — the build continues.

Read the log like a detective. If a step shows a red ❌, click it. The log shows exactly which command failed and the error message. The error message is your best clue — the troubleshooting module maps common messages to fixes. A red ❌ is normal in software work and almost always fixable.

Step 6 — Download and install (5 min)

On the successful run's page, scroll to Artifacts and click the artifact name to download a zip. Unzip it to find the .apk file. Transfer it to your Android phone by email, Google Drive, messaging app or USB cable.

On the phone, open the file from your Files or Downloads app. Android will warn that installing from this source is not allowed — tap Settings, enable Allow from this source, go back and tap Install, then Open. The app requires Android 8.0 or newer.

What you just achieved

You have built and installed a real Android app using a professional cloud build pipeline — the same kind of CI/CD system used by software teams worldwide — without installing developer tools. That is a genuine builder credential.

Security habits

After installing, consider turning "Allow from this source" off again for apps like your file manager or browser, so other unknown apps cannot install silently. Only share APKs that you built or trust, and tell testers where the file came from.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my build-log interpreter. I will paste the steps and any error text from my GitHub Actions run. Explain in simple language what each step does, identify the failed step and the likely cause, and give me the exact browser-only fix to try first, then a second option if that fails.

📚 Glossary

  • Workflow run: one execution of the build instructions
  • Artifact: file produced and stored by a workflow run
  • dist folder: compiled, optimised web app output
  • Capacitor sync: copying the web build into the native project
  • Build log: detailed record of each build step and errors

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 4–6. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Viewing workflow run history; Downloading workflow artifacts.
  • Android Help — Install apps from unknown sources (varies by manufacturer).

quiz.q: After uploading, the repository page shows src, public and package.json but not .github. What should the learner do?
opts: Show hidden files and upload the .github folder
quiz.x: Without .github the build never starts.

quiz.q: Which step compiles the web app into the dist folder?
quiz.x: The web build produces optimised output in dist.

quiz.q: The first build takes eight minutes. What is the MOST likely reason?
opts: GitHub is downloading the full Android toolkit for the first time
quiz.x: First builds download toolchains; later builds are faster.

quiz.q: A step shows a red ❌. What should the learner do FIRST?
opts: Click the failed step and read the error message in the log
quiz.x: The log identifies the failing command and error.

quiz.q: Where is the downloadable APK found after a successful run?
opts: In the Artifacts section at the bottom of the run page
quiz.x: Artifacts store files produced by the workflow.

quiz.q: Android blocks installation with 'not allowed to install unknown apps from this source'. What is the correct response?
opts: Open Settings from the dialog, enable Allow from this source for that app, then install
quiz.x: Permitting installation from the source is normal for non-Play-Store apps.

quiz.q: Which step copies the web build into the Android project?
quiz.x: Capacitor sync moves the web build into the native project.

quiz.q: Why does the course suggest turning 'Allow from this source' off again after installing?
opts: To prevent other unknown apps from installing through that source
quiz.x: Limiting install permissions improves security.

quiz.q: The app installs but crashes on an old phone. What is the likely cause?
opts: The commit message was too short
The phone runs an Android version older than 8.0
quiz.x: The app requires Android 8.0 or newer.

quiz.q: What does the Upload artifact step do?
opts: Uploads code to the Play Store
Stores the built APK so you can download it
quiz.x: It saves the build output as a downloadable artifact.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK III: Releases, Updates & Troubleshooting
modules.d: Public download links, safe updates, version discipline and calm troubleshooting.
modules.body:
Step 7 — Create a public download link (Releases)

Artifacts require a GitHub login to download, so they are not ideal for sharing. A Release creates a permanent public download page anyone can open without an account. On your repository page: Releases → Create a new release → create a tag v1.0.0 → add a title and description ("First public release. Requires Android 8.0+") → Publish release. In this project, publishing the tag triggers a fresh build; about five minutes later the APK appears under Assets. Share the link (github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/your-repo/releases) on WhatsApp or social media, or print it as a QR code.

Step 8 — Making changes forever after

Navigate to any file in your repository (for example src/App.jsx), click the pencil icon, edit it in the browser like a document — your contact information, programme names, colours or text — then Commit changes with a clear message ("Update contact number"). A new APK builds automatically. Make one small change at a time and check the build succeeds before the next change; this makes errors easy to find.

Version discipline: semantic versioning

Versions communicate what changed: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. v1.0.0 → v1.0.1 for small fixes; → v1.1.0 for new features that do not break existing use; → v2.0.0 for major redesigns or breaking changes. Write release notes describing what changed so users and testers know what to expect.

Your safety net: history. Every commit is recorded. If an edit breaks the build, open the file's History, view the previous working version, and restore its content. Never panic about a broken build — the last working version is always there.

Step 9 — Troubleshooting the calm way

  • Red ❌ with "Could not find installation of TypeScript": replace capacitor.config.ts with capacitor.config.json containing the equivalent settings (your instructor provides the contents).
  • "Dependencies lock file is not found": edit the workflow file — remove the cache: npm line and change npm ci to npm install.
  • "No such file or directory: dist": the web build failed earlier — scroll up in the log; usually a typo in your last edit. Revert using file history.
  • Empty Artifacts: the build is still running or failed — check for a ❌.
  • "Allow from this source" missing: the setting location varies by brand; on stock Android try Settings → Apps → Special app access → Install unknown apps.
  • App crashes on open: the phone is probably below Android 8.0 — check Settings → About phone.
  • Uploaded the wrong files: you can delete the repository (Settings → Delete this repository) and start fresh.

The improvement loop

When you finish: test every feature; share the release link with at least three people; watch them install and use the app; note where they get confused; make one improvement; release v1.0.1; repeat. This build–measure–learn loop is how every great app evolves.

Next steps as a builder

Add a README describing your app, its purpose and how to install it. Later steps include custom app icons and names, publishing to the Play Store (requiring an AAB, a developer account and signing), and learning enough code to customise features with AI assistance in Vibe Coding Mastery.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my release manager. I will describe the changes I made to my app since the last release. Recommend the correct semantic version number (patch, minor or major) with reasoning, write clear release notes for testers in English and French, and give me a 5-step test checklist to run on my phone before sharing the release link.

📚 Glossary

  • Release: public, versioned download page
  • Tag: label marking a specific version, e.g., v1.0.0
  • Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbering
  • Release notes: description of what changed in a version
  • File history: record of every version of a file

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 7–9. Team21 Academy.
  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — semver.org.
  • GitHub Docs — Managing releases in a repository.

quiz.q: A teacher wants students without GitHub accounts to download the app. What should the builder create?
opts: A Release with the APK as a public asset
quiz.x: Releases provide public downloads without login.

quiz.q: A builder fixes a typo in the app's text. Which version follows v1.2.0?
quiz.x: Small fixes increment the PATCH number.

quiz.q: A builder adds a new language option without breaking existing features. Which version follows v1.2.1?
quiz.x: New compatible features increment MINOR and reset PATCH.

quiz.q: The build fails with 'Dependencies lock file is not found'. What is the course's fix?
opts: In the workflow file, remove cache: npm and change npm ci to npm install
quiz.x: This adjusts the workflow to install without a lock file.

quiz.q: An edit breaks the build. What is the SAFEST recovery?
opts: Use the file's History to restore the last working version
quiz.x: Version history provides a reliable rollback.

quiz.q: The log says 'No such file or directory: dist'. What does this usually indicate?
opts: The web build failed earlier, often due to an error in the last edit
quiz.x: The dist folder is produced by the web build; its absence points to an earlier failure.

quiz.q: Why does the course recommend making one small change at a time?
opts: If the build breaks, the cause is easy to identify
quiz.x: Small steps isolate problems.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of release notes?
opts: To tell users and testers what changed in each version
quiz.x: Notes communicate changes clearly.

quiz.q: Which describes the improvement loop at the end of the module?
opts: Wait for the Play Store to review
Test, share, observe users, improve, release a new version, repeat
quiz.x: Build–measure–learn drives app improvement.

quiz.q: The error 'Could not find installation of TypeScript' appears. What does the course recommend?
quiz.x: Using the JSON configuration avoids the TypeScript dependency.

modules.t: Your First Business Automation: Form → Instant Email
modules.d: Build a real automation with Make or Zapier, mapping form data into a personalised email.
modules.body:
What we are building

Someone fills out your Google Form → the automation sees the submission → they instantly receive a personalised thank-you email. No manual work. Real example: a yoga instructor's class registration automatically sends class details, location and time to each person who signs up.

Before you start

You need a Google account, Gmail to send replies, a Google Form, and a free account on Make (make.com) or Zapier (zapier.com).

Step 1 — Create the form

Go to Google Forms → create a blank form (e.g., "Customer Inquiry Form"). Add at least two short-answer questions: "What is your name?" and "What is your email?". The email field is essential — it is how the automation knows whom to reply to. Consider using response validation to require a valid email format. Preview the form to test it.

Option A — Make

  1. Log in to Make → Create a new scenario.
  2. Add the trigger module: search Google Forms → Watch Responses → create a connection to your Google account and allow access → select your form.
  3. Click + to add an action: Gmail → Send an Email → connect Gmail.
  4. To: click in the field and select the form's email answer from the mapping panel (the data the trigger provides).
  5. Subject: "Thank you for your inquiry!"; Content: your message — insert the respondent's name by selecting the Name field from the mapping panel.
  6. Save → Run once → submit the form yourself → check the email arrives.
  7. Turn the scenario ON and set its schedule (how often Make checks for new responses).

Option B — Zapier

  1. Log in to Zapier → Create → Zap.
  2. Trigger: Google Forms → New Form Response → connect your account → choose the form → submit a test response → Test trigger.
  3. Action: Gmail → Send Email → connect Gmail.
  4. Map To to the email answer; write the subject; in the body insert the Name field from the form data.
  5. Test action → check your inbox → name the Zap ("Form auto-reply") → Publish.
The most common mistake. Typing an email address or name into the field instead of selecting the mapped data. If you type text, every email goes to the same address with the same name. Always use the field selector to map form data.

Make or Zapier?

Both connect thousands of apps and offer free plans with usage limits. Zapier is often considered the simplest for beginners; Make offers a visual scenario builder that many find powerful for multi-step workflows and a generous free tier. Both count usage (Zapier in tasks; Make in operations or credits), and plans and limits change — check current pricing before building many automations.

Troubleshooting

  • No email sent: check that the Gmail connection shows as connected, the form has an email field, the scenario or Zap is ON, and check spam.
  • Name or email missing: you typed text instead of mapping the form field.
  • Google connection error: disconnect and reconnect, and confirm you are using the Google account that owns the form.

Responsible automation

Tell people in the form what will happen with their data and that they will receive an email. Collect only what you need, and protect respondents' information. Automated emails must still be accurate and respectful — test them as carefully as messages you write by hand.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my automation tutor. I want to build a Google Form → Gmail auto-reply in [Make or Zapier]. Walk me through each step one at a time, waiting for me to confirm. Then help me write a warm, bilingual (English and French) auto-reply email that includes the respondent's name and the next steps, and give me a 4-point test checklist before I switch it on.

📚 Glossary

  • Scenario / Zap: an automation in Make / Zapier
  • Module: a single step in a Make scenario
  • Mapping panel: where you select data from earlier steps
  • Task / operation: usage units counted by Zapier / Make
  • Response validation: form rule requiring correctly formatted answers

📖 References

  • Team21 Academy, No-Code Automation Guide: Automate Google Form Submissions with Instant Email Replies.
  • Make Help Center and Make Academy (make.com).
  • Zapier Help Center (zapier.com/help).
  • Google Forms Help — response validation.

quiz.q: Every automated reply goes to the builder's own email address with the name 'John'. What is the MOST likely cause?
opts: The builder typed fixed text instead of mapping the form's email and name fields
quiz.x: Fields must be mapped from trigger data, not typed.

quiz.q: Why must the form include an email question?
opts: The automation needs the respondent's address to send the reply
quiz.x: The email answer is mapped to the 'To' field.

quiz.q: In Make, what is the trigger module for this automation?
quiz.x: Watching form responses starts the scenario.

quiz.q: A Zap is built and tested but no emails arrive for real submissions. What should be checked FIRST?
opts: Whether the Zap was published and turned ON
quiz.x: Unpublished or OFF automations do not run.

quiz.q: Which statement about usage is MOST accurate?
opts: Both count usage (tasks or operations/credits) with plan limits that change, so check current pricing
Both tools are unlimited on free plans
quiz.x: Usage units and plan limits apply and change.

quiz.q: A Google connection error appears in Make. What does the guide suggest?
opts: Disconnect and reconnect, using the Google account that owns the form
quiz.x: Reconnecting with the correct account resolves most connection errors.

quiz.q: Which practice reflects responsible automation?
opts: Collecting as much data as possible
Telling respondents what will happen with their data and collecting only what is needed
quiz.x: Transparency and minimisation protect respondents.

quiz.q: What does response validation on the email question do?
opts: Requires respondents to enter a correctly formatted email address
quiz.x: Validation reduces bad addresses that would break replies.

quiz.q: In the trigger–action model, 'send a thank-you email' is the:
quiz.x: The action is what happens after the trigger.

quiz.q: Why should a builder submit the form themselves before turning the automation ON?
opts: To test that the trigger, mapping and email work correctly
quiz.x: Testing confirms the automation behaves as intended.

modules.d: Multi-step workflows, filters, logging, error handling — and your capstone project.
modules.body:
From one automation to a system

Your first automation proved the trigger–action–mapping pattern. Real businesses chain several steps: record every submission, notify the team, route requests to the right person, and follow up automatically. Good design keeps these workflows reliable, understandable and safe.

Common building blocks

  • Logging to Google Sheets: add each submission as a row — a simple database for tracking leads, registrations or orders.
  • Notifications: send yourself or your team a message (email, Slack, Telegram, or SMS via a provider) when something important arrives.
  • Filters: continue only when conditions are met — e.g., only send the VIP email if the budget answer is above a threshold.
  • Routers / paths: send different responses depending on answers — e.g., French speakers receive the French email.
  • Calendar events: create appointments automatically from booking forms.
  • Delays and follow-ups: send a reminder two days later or a follow-up after a week.
  • AI steps: both platforms can call AI models to summarise, classify or draft text inside an automation — powerful, but outputs should be reviewed when they reach customers.

Designing before building

Sketch the workflow on paper or a whiteboard: trigger, each step, conditions, and what happens if something fails. Name each step clearly. Ask: What data does each step need? Where does it come from? Who receives what, in which language? This five-minute sketch prevents hours of rebuilding.

Plan for failure. Automations fail silently if no one is watching: a disconnected account, a changed form question, a full mailbox. Turn on error notifications, check the run history weekly, and test after changing any connected form or sheet. Both Make and Zapier provide execution histories and error alerts — use them.

Data, privacy and trust

Automations move personal data between services. Collect only what you need, tell people how it will be used, restrict access to sheets containing personal data, and remove data you no longer need. Do not send marketing to people who have not agreed. When AI steps process customer messages, check the platform's data terms.

Cost and maintenance

Each step consumes usage units on most plans, and frequently-checking triggers increase usage. Estimate monthly volume before scaling, combine steps where sensible, and document what each automation does and who owns it — so it can be maintained when you are busy or when a team member takes over.

Your capstone project

Complete both builder credentials:

  1. App: your project built through GitHub Actions, installed on a phone, published as a public Release (v1.0.0), with one improvement shipped as v1.0.1 after testing with at least three people, and a README describing the app.
  2. Automation: a working multi-step workflow for a real or realistic business — at minimum a form trigger, a Google Sheets log, a personalised email reply and one filter or route — with a sketch of the design, a test record, error notifications enabled and a short description of how personal data is protected.

Submit links, screenshots and a one-page reflection on what you learned and what you would build next. Your mentor reviews it for functionality, reliability and responsible data use.
